Divine Will
dih-VYN wil
noun
From divine + will; the will of God, distinguished by the theologians into His secret and revealed will.

📖 Biblical Definition

The divine will is the will of God, by which He purposes and accomplishes all things according to His own good pleasure. The theologians distinguish two aspects, both taught in Scripture. There is the secret or decretive will of God—His eternal, sovereign, and unchangeable purpose, by which He has foreordained whatsoever comes to pass; this will is always accomplished, for who hath resisted His will? He doeth according to His will in the army of heaven and among the inhabitants of the earth, and none can stay His hand. And there is the revealed or preceptive will of God—His commandments, what He has made known of our duty in His word; this will is often disobeyed by sinners, for men break His commandments daily, yet it is the rule of our obedience. The secret will is the rule of God’s actions; the revealed will is the rule of ours. We are not to pry into the secret things, which belong unto the LORD, but to do the things that are revealed, which belong to us and to our children. The distinction guards against great errors: it preserves the sovereignty of God, who accomplishes His whole purpose, and the responsibility of man, who is bound by the commands; and it forbids us to excuse our sin by appeal to the decree, or to charge God with the evil men do. The dictionary honors the doctrine of the divine will as a key to the harmony of Scripture: God ordains all things by His secret will, and yet sincerely commands all men by His revealed will, and is the author of no man’s sin.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

The will of God, distinguished into His secret will (the decree that ordains all) and His revealed will (His commands, the rule of our duty); the key to sovereignty and responsibility.

expand to see more

DIVINE WILL, the will of God, by which He purposes and accomplishes all.

The secret or decretive will: His eternal purpose, always accomplished.

The revealed or preceptive will: His commands, the rule of our duty.

The secret things belong to God; the revealed, to us (Deu 29:29).

Guards both the sovereignty of God and the responsibility of man.

📖 Key Scripture

Deu 29:29 — "The secret things belong unto the LORD our God: but those things which are revealed belong unto us and to our children for ever, that we may do all the words of this law."

Dan 4:35 — "And all the inhabitants of the earth are reputed as nothing: and he doeth according to his will in the army of heaven, and among the inhabitants of the earth: and none can stay his hand, or say unto him, What doest thou?"

Eph 1:11 — "In whom also we have obtained an inheritance, being predestinated according to the purpose of him who worketh all things after the counsel of his own will:"

1Th 4:3 — "For this is the will of God, even your sanctification, that ye should abstain from fornication:"

⚠️ Modern Corruption

God’s will is flattened to one thing, pitting sovereignty against command; Scripture’s distinction of secret and revealed will upholds both, excusing no sin.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The corruption is the flattening of the divine will into a single undistinguished thing, which then pits the sovereignty of God against His commands. Some seize the decree to deny that God truly commands or sincerely calls all men; others seize the commands to deny that God ordains all things; and the impenitent seize the decree to excuse their sin—if God willed it, how am I guilty? The confusion breeds error on every side.

The principle to recover is the biblical distinction of God’s secret and revealed will. By His secret will He worketh all things after the counsel of His own will (Eph 1:11) and doeth according to His will in heaven and earth, and none can stay His hand (Dan 4:35); this is the rule of His actions, and it is always done. By His revealed will He commands our duty—this is the will of God, even your sanctification (1 Thess 4:3); this is the rule of our obedience, and it is often broken by sinners. The secret things belong to God; the revealed belong to us, that we may do them (Deu 29:29). The distinction upholds both God’s sovereignty and man’s responsibility, forbids the sinner to hide behind the decree, and clears God of the evil men do: He ordains all, commands the good, and is the author of no man’s sin.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

Divine + will; the will of God in its secret (decretive) and revealed (preceptive) aspects, upholding His sovereignty and man’s responsibility.

expand to see more

Divine will — the will of God, secret and revealed.

Secret will: His decree, worked after the counsel of His will (Eph 1:11).

Revealed will: His commands, the rule of our duty (1Th 4:3).

The secret things belong to God; the revealed, to us (Deu 29:29).

Upholds God’s sovereignty and man’s responsibility alike.

Usage

"The divine will is distinguished into God’s secret and revealed will."

"By His secret will He worketh all things after the counsel of His own will."

"The secret things belong to the LORD; the revealed, to us, that we may obey."
